name: World-Building and Continuity
title: World-Building and Continuity
answer: World-building and continuity is the craft of keeping a fictional setting coherent across many pieces of work, whether that is a novel series, a game franchise, a television writers room or a tabletop campaign. It covers places, timelines, factions, languages, technology, magic systems and the small facts that readers notice when they contradict each other. In practice the work sits between the writer, the editor and the production team, and it is as much record keeping as invention. The rise of generative tools has widened the field, because a setting can now be extended into images, voices and video, not only prose.

sections.body: World-building and continuity is the craft of keeping a fictional setting coherent across many pieces of work, whether that is a novel series, a game franchise, a television writers room or a tabletop campaign. It covers places, timelines, factions, languages, technology, magic systems and the small facts that readers notice when they contradict each other. In practice the work sits between the writer, the editor and the production team, and it is as much record keeping as invention. The rise of generative tools has widened the field, because a setting can now be extended into images, voices and video, not only prose.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most continuity work runs on a mix of documents and databases: a story bible, a wiki, spreadsheets of names and dates, and increasingly a retrieval system that lets a writer query the canon rather than search it by hand. Image and video generators are used to visualise characters, costumes and locations, and this site tracks 1000 live image generation models and 1000 video models, so the choice of tool is itself a continuity decision. Audio models, of which 2000 are tracked here, matter when a setting has invented languages, accents or recurring voices. The general purpose assistants among the 850 AI tools tracked on the site are often the first thing a small team reaches for, before any dedicated canon database exists.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method is to write the canon down first and generate second, so that a model is conditioned on approved material rather than asked to invent freely. Teams build a reference set of descriptions, images and sample dialogue, then use retrieval to pull the relevant entries into a prompt before a scene, a portrait or a line of dialogue is produced. A human editor still checks every output against the bible, because models will happily produce a plausible detail that contradicts an established one. Versioning matters as much as generation: when a fact changes, the change has to propagate to every downstream asset. The glossary of 688 terms on this site reflects how much shared vocabulary the field has accumulated around exactly this kind of pipeline.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance are live questions for any setting that mixes human and generated material. A franchise owner needs to know which assets are human authored, which are generated, and under what terms each can be used, and that record has to survive staff turnover. The 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, 18 of them involving AI music services, show that these questions are being tested rather than settled. Fan works, licensed tie ins and adaptations each carry their own permissions, and a continuity database often becomes the place where those permissions are recorded. Nothing here is legal advice, and teams typically route these questions to counsel rather than resolve them internally.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward canon as a queryable system rather than a document, with retrieval, versioning and generation sharing one source of truth. That makes consistency cheaper to maintain but raises the cost of a mistake, because an error in the source propagates everywhere at once. Expect more work on provenance metadata, so that any generated image, voice or scene can be traced back to the entry it came from. Smaller studios will likely benefit most, since the same tooling that a large franchise uses to police continuity can help a two person team keep a first series straight. The open question is authorship, and how much of a world a writer is willing to let a model fill in.
